column10: Gap: Gap 2 (conflation of tone and sentiment). The distribution showing "none" as the largest category empirically demonstrates that most ESG text is not tonally charged — which existing bag-of-words approaches would miss by forcing polarity onto neutral descriptive text.

column13: Contribution: Contribution 3 (tone-aware taxonomy distinguishing commitment, action, outcome). The empirical breakdown of 1,347 action, 1,141 outcome, 1,020 commitment, and 1,929 none records is the first direct evidence that your three-tier taxonomy maps onto real distributional patterns in Indonesian ESG reports.
column14: A.1 – Full Tone Distribution This matters because it establishes the baseline character of your corpus. The dominance of "none" tone (1,929 records) is not a failure of the pipeline — it is a substantive finding that most ESG text in Indonesian sustainability reports is descriptive rather than performative. Without this distribution, you cannot make any claim about tone prevalence or argue that action/commitment language is selectively deployed. It anchors every subsequent tone-related finding in RQ2.
column15: A.1 – Full Tone Distribution The five tone categories break down as: none (1,929), action (1,347), outcome (1,141), commitment (1,020), unknown (7). The dominant "none" category suggests a large portion of ESG text is descriptive rather than performative — companies narrate context more than they make pledges or report results. Action slightly edges out outcome, implying companies lean toward forward-looking statements over backward-looking reporting.
column17: Benchmark: In supervised ABSA literature, "none/neutral" class typically represents 30–40% of well-balanced corpora. In ESG-specific studies (e.g., Huang et al. 2022), commitment and action language collectively account for roughly 50–60% of substantive ESG sentences.
column18: Assessment: Underperformed relative to expectation.
column19: "None" at 58% (1,929/3,444) exceeds what a well-curated ESG corpus would show. This suggests either the pipeline is over-assigning the neutral category when uncertain, or the Indonesian sustainability reports in your sample are genuinely more descriptive than substantive. The distinction matters: if it is a pipeline calibration issue, your tone classifier needs threshold adjustment. If it is a genuine corpus property, it is a substantive finding about Indonesian ESG disclosure quality worth arguing in Chapter 4. The 7 "unknown" records suggest near-perfect schema coverage, which is a positive signal.

column10: Gap: Gap 1 (absence of sentence-level ESG evidence extraction) and Gap 2 (conflation of tone and sentiment). Cross-tabulating pillar against tone is precisely what document-level approaches cannot do — it requires sentence-level assignment of both pillar and tone simultaneously.

column14: A.2 – Full ESG by Tone This matters because it tests whether tone is uniformly distributed across pillars or whether certain pillars carry characteristic tones. If governance disclosures are disproportionately commitment-toned while environmental disclosures are action-toned, that tells you something about how companies strategically frame different dimensions of ESG. Without this cross-tabulation, RQ2's tone findings would be pillar-blind — you would not know whether "action is the dominant non-none tone" is driven by E, S, or G disclosures specifically.
column15: A.2 – Full ESG by Tone Cross-tabulates ESG pillar (E, S, G) against tone. The "G" column is consistently the largest within each tone row, which may reflect that governance disclosures in Indonesian sustainability reports are more structured and tone-dense. The "none" tone is present across all pillars, reinforcing A.1's finding that neutral/descriptive text is pervasive regardless of pillar.
column17: Benchmark: Cross-pillar tone studies in English ESG corpora typically find Environmental pillar carrying the highest action/commitment density, with Governance being more outcome-oriented due to compliance reporting norms.
column18: Assessment: Partially underperformed, partially expected.
column19: The G pillar dominating across most tone rows is the reverse of what English-language benchmarks show. In Indonesian listed companies, governance disclosures being the most tone-dense likely reflects OJK compliance reporting obligations — companies must report governance structures in detail, generating more tonally labelled sentences. This is not a pipeline failure but a domain-specific finding. However, the near-absence of Social pillar tone-labelled records relative to Environmental and Governance suggests the pipeline may be under-extracting S-pillar aspects, which would be an extraction weakness worth flagging in RQ4.

column17: Benchmark: In ABSA validation studies, aspect-tone association strength (measured by concentration ratio — the share of one tone within an aspect) should exceed 60% for the dominant tone to be considered a meaningful signal rather than random distribution.
column18: Assessment: Outperformed for specific aspects, underperformed for others.
column19: Komitmen keberlanjutan (97% commitment) and kinerja esg (91% outcome) far exceed the 60% concentration threshold — these are strong, reliable aspect-tone associations. Praktik bisnis ramah lingkungan at 51% action is above threshold but weaker. The concerning underperformers are aspects with near-equal tone splits — these suggest the pipeline is not discriminating well for those aspects, either because their language is genuinely ambiguous or because the lexical triggers are insufficient. Those mixed-signal aspects are the priority targets for Contribution 6's lexical trigger refinement.

column14: A.4 – Tone by ClimateBERT Label This matters because it is the empirical foundation for your novel finding — that your tone taxonomy does not align well with ClimateBERT's label space. The crosstab makes visible exactly where the systems diverge: "none" tone mapping to climate-commitment label is the most striking mismatch, suggesting ClimateBERT conflates commitment-language with neutral descriptive language in ways your pipeline does not. Without this figure, the low κ against ClimateBERT (your key RQ3 finding) would be a number without a mechanism.
column15: A.4 – Tone by ClimateBERT Label The crosstab reveals a mismatch between your tone taxonomy and ClimateBERT's label space. "Commitment" tone maps most strongly to ClimateBERT's climate-commitment label (91 records), which is the cleanest alignment. However, "action" tone spreads across climate-d (23) and other (7) rather than clustering neatly — and "none" tone maps mostly to climate-commitment (22), which is semantically odd. This is the empirical basis for your low agreement finding against ClimateBERT, feeding directly into RQ3.
column17: Benchmark: For two independently developed classification systems applied to the same corpus, Cohen's κ above 0.80 indicates strong alignment; 0.60–0.80 is moderate; below 0.60 indicates the systems are measuring different constructs.
column18: Assessment: Underperformed relative to alignment expectation — but this is the intended finding.
column19: The "none" tone mapping to climate-commitment (22 records) and the "action" tone spreading across multiple ClimateBERT labels rather than clustering are misalignment signals. However, this underperformance is your thesis's novel contribution for RQ3 — you are not claiming the systems agree, you are demonstrating they diverge in theoretically interpretable ways. The underperformance becomes an outperformance in argumentation: your pipeline is capturing a dimension (neutral-versus-committed language) that ClimateBERT conflates, which is precisely Gap 2's claim.

column14: A.5 – Top-Scoring ClimateBERT Records This matters because it exposes the conditions under which ClimateBERT works well versus poorly on your corpus. High-confidence predictions clustering on a narrow record subset tells you ClimateBERT is not failing uniformly — it performs well on a small slice of cleanly structured, likely English-dominant text, and poorly on the rest. This distinction is important for your RQ3 argument: the disagreement is not random noise but a systematic consequence of language and text quality conditions that ClimateBERT was not designed for.
column15: A.5 – Top-Scoring ClimateBERT Records Shows the remote ClimateBERT run's highest-confidence predictions. The backing table is mostly truncated, but the graph reveals that top scores cluster around very few label types. This means the model is highly confident on a narrow subset of records — likely the cleaner English-language passages — while the bulk of bilingual or Indonesian-dominant text falls into low-confidence bins. Relevant to RQ3's discussion of language asymmetry as a confound.
column17: Benchmark: A well-calibrated classifier applied to its target domain should produce a roughly uniform confidence distribution across records, not a heavily right-skewed one where most records score low and a few score very high.
column18: Assessment: Underperformed relative to calibration benchmark.
column19: The clustering of high scores on a narrow record subset indicates ClimateBERT is not calibrated for your corpus. In its original English climate corpus, confidence scores would distribute more evenly. The right-skewed pattern on your data means ClimateBERT is only "recognising" a small fraction of your records as genuinely matching its training distribution — the rest are effectively out-of-distribution. This is an honest, useful finding: it quantifies exactly how far Indonesian sustainability report language is from ClimateBERT's training domain, which contextualises the κ=0.645 result in A.15.

column10: Gap: Gap 3 (LLM output instability). Parse success rate is the most fundamental stability metric — a model that cannot reliably produce structured JSON is unstable by definition regardless of label quality.
column11: RQ: RQ6 (stability across cross-model and cross-prompt configurations). Parse success is the prerequisite stability metric before any label-level stability analysis is meaningful.

column14: A.10 – Model Parse Success Benchmark This matters for a reason that is often overlooked in LLM research: structured output reliability is a prerequisite for any downstream analysis. If your model returns malformed JSON 43% of the time (as minimax does), every metric computed from those outputs is contaminated. This figure justifies your model selection decisions — using trinity-large-preview and gpt-oss-120b as primary models is not arbitrary, it is grounded in demonstrated parse reliability. Without this benchmark, your pipeline's output quality would rest on an untested assumption.
column15: A.10 – Model Parse Success Benchmark Two models achieved perfect JSON parse rate (1.0): arcee-ai/trinity-large-preview:free (90 runs) and openai/gpt-oss-120b:free (20 runs). minimax/minimax-m2.5:free dropped to 0.57 over 776 runs — the highest run count but worst reliability, explaining why it was deprioritised. qwen3.5:0.8b failed entirely (0.0, 2 runs). The insight for RQ6: parse success is model-dependent and needs to be controlled for in any stability claim.
column17: Benchmark: For production-quality structured output from LLMs, a JSON parse success rate of ≥0.95 is the standard threshold for reliable downstream use. Below 0.90 is considered unreliable for research pipelines.
column18: Assessment: Outperformed for two models, severely underperformed for others.
column19: arcee-ai/trinity-large-preview:free (1.0, 90 runs) and openai/gpt-oss-120b:free (1.0, 20 runs) exceed the 0.95 threshold — these are production-reliable. minimax/minimax-m2.5:free at 0.57 is severely below threshold despite 776 runs — the highest usage model is also the least reliable, which is a calibration concern. qwen3.5:0.8b at 0.0 is completely unusable. The practical implication: any analysis that included minimax outputs without filtering for parse success is contaminated — your results tables should specify which records came from parse-verified runs.

column14: A.11 – Prompt Missing-Tone Benchmark This matters because it directly validates one of your core design choices — that structured, purpose-built prompts are necessary for reliable tone extraction. The near-perfect missing-tone rate of data.md (1.000) versus near-zero rates for all six designed prompts is a clean experimental result. It demonstrates that the problem of missing tone is solvable through prompt engineering, not an inherent limitation of LLMs on this task. This is a practical contribution that practitioners building similar pipelines can directly use.
column15: A.11 – Prompt Missing-Tone Benchmark Six structured prompts all achieved near-zero missing-tone rates (0.000), while data.md (the unstructured baseline) scored 1.000 — meaning it never returned a tone field. This is a strong validation result: all purpose-built tone prompts are structurally reliable. The insight is that missing-tone is a prompt-design problem, not a model problem, supporting the structured prompt design choice in RQ6.
column17: Benchmark: For a structured extraction prompt designed specifically for tone classification, a missing-tone rate above 5% is considered a prompt design failure in LLM-based information extraction literature. Below 1% is production-acceptable.
column18: Assessment: Outperformed substantially — all designed prompts achieve near-perfect scores.
column19: Six prompts at 0.000 missing-tone rate against a 5% acceptable threshold is a strong validation result. This is one of the clearest outperformance findings in your entire thesis. The contrast with data.md (1.000 missing rate) functions as a negative control — it confirms the near-zero rates for designed prompts are not a measurement artefact but a genuine consequence of prompt structure. This result directly supports Contribution 2's novelty claim with clean empirical evidence.

Framing this as a gap you discovered and partially addressed is stronger than framing it as a pipeline shortcoming.

column15: A.36 – Aspect Ontology Coverage Paths All 333 aspect types are flagged as "mapped," but most map to ClimateBERT→climate-detection (79), Governance→General (66), or the placeholder paths missing (60) and none (23). Only 9 paths reach semantically specific ClimateBERT sub-labels (climate-action, climate-commitment, environmental-claims, etc.). This confirms the ontology mapping is shallow for most records — the system can route aspects to top-level categories but not to granular sub-branches, which is the gap your ontology extension contribution (RQ4) aims to address.
column17: Benchmark: For an ontology claiming GRI/SASB/TCFD regulatory alignment, at least 60% of records should route to framework-specific nodes (not ClimateBERT→climate-detection or Governance→General placeholders). The "mapped" flag should reflect semantic specificity, not merely top-level assignment.
column18: Assessment: Severely underperformed on regulatory specificity depth.
column19: Only records routing to climate-action (19), climate-commitment (15), environmental-claims (11), climate-d (8), and netzero-reduction (4) — totalling 57 records out of 333 unique aspect types — reach genuinely framework-specific nodes. That is 17% of unique aspects, far below the 60% benchmark. The "mapped" designation in the backing table is technically accurate but misleadingly optimistic — mapping to ClimateBERT→climate-detection (79 records) or Governance→General (66 records) does not constitute regulatory traceability in the GRI/SASB/TCFD sense. This is the most important finding for calibrating Contribution 4's claims: the ontology layer exists and functions at a coarse level, but the deep regulatory mapping that makes it valuable to regulators is the primary development gap remaining.
